title: An Inflection Point for Prediction Markets

content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

The day before Donald Trump’s second State of the Union address, the former Representative George Santos shared a video of himself saying, in no uncertain terms, that he was “going to be there.” The next day, he didn’t show up. According to the prediction-market company Kalshi, that was the plan—the firm alleged that he made roughly $17,000 by betting on the platform that he wouldn’t appear at the speech. Kalshi flagged the wager to federal authorities, and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the agency that regulates prediction markets, fined Santos over it in July. On Monday, Kalshi doubled down, levying a fine of its own and giving him the platform’s first-ever lifetime ban.

Prediction-market companies, which let users make bets on the outcomes of all sorts of real-world events, have fully entered the mainstream over the past few years. You can find their logos at major sporting events, on cable-news broadcasts, and at awards shows. They’re easy to access and, thanks to a recent advertising blitz, essentially ubiquitous. Trading volumes on Kalshi and Polymarket, the two market leaders, have exceeded $200 billion and $100 billion this year, respectively. But these companies have strenuously resisted the idea that they should be thought of as gambling platforms. “I just don’t really know what this has to do with gambling,” Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said of his company last year. (By avoiding this classification, prediction markets have also been able to operate in states where sports betting is banned.) Instead, Kalshi and Polymarket have suggested that their platforms are digital oracles: potent indicators of what the future might hold, fueled by the wisdom of the crowd.

In recent months, a nascent crackdown on insider trading has been exposing a fundamental tension in these companies’ guiding principles. If the goal is to create fair markets and not get targeted by the government, then they must enforce a ban on insider trading, as U.S. regulators already do. But if the goal is forecasting—aligning these markets’ odds with what’s really going to happen in the world—then allowing bettors to trade on inside information could actually benefit these platforms. This, at least, was once the thinking of Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan, who described his platform last year as “the most accurate thing we have as mankind right now, until someone else creates some sort of a super crystal ball.” In response to a question about his approach to preventing insider trading, he said in November that Polymarket “creates this financial incentive for people to go and divulge the information to the market”—theoretically creating more accurate projections.

This may help explain why Polymarket has taken so long to clamp down on insider trading. The company didn’t explicitly ban the practice until March, nearly six years after its founding. Kalshi took a different tack: When I reached out to the company in January, its representatives stressed that insider trading was unambiguously prohibited. (But the question of which offenders are penalized—and what those punishments look like—still seems to be decided on a case-by-case basis.)

This year, both companies have been ramping up their enforcement efforts. The shift began back in January, when The Wall Street Journal reported that, in the lead-up to the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, an unknown trader had made more than $400,000 betting that Maduro would soon be out of power. To many observers, it certainly looked like insider trading—and lawmakers from both parties began pushing for stricter regulation. A few months later, Polymarket notified the Department of Justice that one of the soldiers involved in the operation had allegedly placed the wager, and the agency indicted him for trading on nonpublic information (he has pleaded not guilty).

According to a spokesperson for Polymarket, the company’s insider-trading investigations have led to “nearly 100 referrals to law enforcement,” and its work on the Maduro bets and on a separate case involving a Google employee resulted in the “first and second prediction markets insider trading cases charged in the United States.” This week, in addition to the Santos ban, Kalshi announced several new settlements with public figures accused of insider trading on its platform, including a North Carolinian candidate for the House who has admitted to betting on her own race. (“I bet on myself,” she wrote in an emailed statement. “It was a dumb mistake, and as soon as I learned there was an issue, I worked to make it right.”) And this past weekend, Trump’s longtime teleprompter operator paid $172,000 to settle the CFTC’s claims that he was betting on the individual words that the president would use in his speeches—claims first made by Kalshi.

Regulators don’t have a unified approach to this sector. As The New York Times points out, 20 states are now waging legal battles over whether these companies should be subject to the same laws as online sportsbooks. In an apparent defense of the industry, the CFTC has sued some of the states suing prediction-market companies for infringing on federal jurisdiction. Polymarket’s international platform, which runs on the blockchain, is off-limits to U.S. traders and isn’t bound by the CFTC’s rules on insider trading.

But even as major legal questions remain unresolved, what’s indisputable is that insider trading is a red line for U.S regulators. Polymarket’s and Kalshi’s stricter enforcement of those rules may help keep them in the federal government’s good graces, and the appearance of fairness may also prevent people from betting elsewhere. But in taking these steps, these businesses will have to reckon with how they present themselves. They can cling to the idea that they’re not gambling platforms—but regulators may not always see it that way.

Today’s News

  1. The United States and Iran exchanged their heaviest attacks since July, with American forces striking Iran’s southern coast and Tehran retaliating against U.S. targets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, and Iraq; U.S. officials said that initial assessments showed no American casualties. Iranian officials said that the latest U.S. strikes killed 18 people, including four at a wedding party, and injured 108.
  2. Jurors in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial said for the second time that they were deadlocked on whether she is criminally responsible for killing her three children in 2023, when, she claims, she was experiencing postpartum psychosis. The judge instructed the jury, now on its fifth day of deliberations, to keep trying to reach a verdict.
  3. Senator Ed Markey defeated Representative Seth Moulton in the Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary last night, winning about 65 percent of the vote; he will face Republican John Deaton in November.

Evening Read

Guillermo Arias / AFP / Getty

The Truth About American Food Safety

By Daniel Engber

The phrase When it rains, it pours isn’t one you like to see applied to outbreaks of foodborne illness, yet here we are. The summer started with a diarrhea-causing parasite called Cyclospora cayetanensis, which infested iceberg lettuce. Then came news of Shiga toxin–producing bacteria in organic frozen berries, and a Salmonella outbreak linked to Whole Foods guacamole that eventually got traced to tainted jalapeños. (Pico de gallo, salsa fresca, and a variety of spicy dips have also been implicated.) Ricotta-style cheese was recalled for Listeria. Both Salmonella and E. coli were found in products from the aptly named Everything Sprouts. And 10,000 cases of lightly fried tofu were flagged for potential contamination with printing ink.

This flood of food-contamination events comes at just the time when our systems to prevent such outbreaks may be hobbled.

title: The Met’s Other Failure
summary: The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s announcement this week that it is canceling next year’s exhibition on the fashion of John Galliano perhaps shouldn’t have come as a surprise. content:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s announcement this week that it is canceling next year’s exhibition on the fashion of John Galliano perhaps shouldn’t have come as a surprise. From the start, Galliano was a controversial pick for the museum’s Costume Institute, which launches its new show each year with the splashy Met Gala. In 2011, he lost his job as creative director of Dior after a video surfaced of him making a drunken anti-Semitic rant; later that year, a French court found him guilty of the crime of making anti-Semitic and anti-Asian insults. The New York Times also recently described claims that Galliano had made anti-Semitic comments during an outburst in 2019. (Through a spokesperson, Galliano denied the 2019 episode.)

But not long after his Dior exit, Galliano—who has always traded on his bad-boy image while producing clothes of astounding beauty and theatricality—was welcomed back into the industry. After so publicly hitting rock-bottom, the designer, who said addiction to drugs and alcohol led to the rants, apologized and went to rehab. Maison Margiela then hired him. Celebrities such as Zendaya wore his designs; this year, the fast-fashion retailer Zara announced a partnership with him to great excitement. Anna Wintour, Vogue’s global editorial director and the Met Gala’s chair, also happens to be his longtime friend and champion. In the process of planning the Met show, Galliano, Wintour, and Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute’s curator, consulted with Jewish leaders, and the exhibition itself intended to—as the museum initially announced in July—explore how the designer’s “derogatory conduct” had “fundamentally altered his career and public reception.”

[Read: Yet another wasted Met Gala]

Those efforts did little to assuage wider public opinion. Museum donors threatened to pull funding; the speaker of the New York city council called the choice of Galliano a “serious mistake.” On Monday, the museum released a statement saying that the show “will not proceed as planned.” It was, Wintour said in the statement, “the right decision.”

It is also a blow to the museum and its reputation that could have been avoided. For most of the Costume Institute’s 80-year history, it has followed an unofficial rule: Don’t do a solo show about a living designer—because such an exhibition could be seen as a form of advertising instead of scholarship, especially if the designer has curatorial input. Although such shows are now commonplace, the Met’s fashion wing has always prided itself on “setting the standard” for conservation and collection, and has devoted only two exhibitions to living designers: Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017. Both were controversial exceptions to long-standing norms intended to separate cultural analysis from commercialism.

Putting on a museum exhibition of Galliano’s work, even while interrogating his past behavior, was always going to be ethically dicey because the designer still stands to benefit from the publicity and prestige that the show bestows. This saga suggests that the Costume Institute, and perhaps all fashion museums, should forgo retrospectives of living artists—and revisit why rules discouraging them were necessary to begin with.

Museums have been routinely collecting and displaying clothes as a branch of the decorative arts since the 19th century, but early fashion exhibits typically featured only historical dress. Contemporary fashion was considered insufficiently artistic, and highlighting it was seen as overly promotional. But as fashion designers became household names in the 1960s, more contemporary pieces found their way into thematic exhibitions. Usually, the items were in shows featuring the work of several designers, including at the Met, which minimized the appearance of endorsing a particular label.

The Costume Institute, which opened to the public in 1946, didn’t devote an entire show to an individual living designer until 1983, when Diana Vreeland—a former Vogue editor in chief—curated a retrospective of Yves Saint Laurent’s work in honor of his label’s 25th anniversary. Saint Laurent was involved in the exhibition and attended the opening fundraiser, both of which were underwritten by the firm that had long designed his textiles. The decision was contentious. Critics argued that it canonized a designer whose work had not yet stood the test of time, while blurring the boundary between art and advertising.

The general public, though, was clearly captivated: The show drew more than 125,000 visitors in just its first month at a time when the average Met exhibition drew 500,000 visitors a year, Women’s Wear Daily reported. Despite its popularity, the experiment was not repeated under the next curator, or the next. Indeed, the Times later reported that the Costume Institute had adopted an “unofficial policy” of not doing monographic shows on living designers due to the “charges of commercialism” that the exhibition drew.

Designers, however, took note of the public’s growing interest in fashion heritage and realized that their own histories could be a valuable source of design inspiration and cultural capital. In 1987, Dior created an archives department; most major fashion labels followed. Fashion-industry archivists started competing with museum curators to buy back their own vintage pieces at auction. Some fashion houses founded their own museums. Others turned their archives into touring exhibitions, large on spectacle and light on scholarship.

[Read: Confessions of a costume curator]

By no coincidence, over the course of the 1990s, fashion studies gained traction as an academic discipline. “Suddenly, fashion was about identity, the body, gender, power, and visual representation,” Valerie Steele, a fashion historian and curator, wrote in Reinvention and Restlessness, a book created for an exhibition at the Museum at FIT. Fashion not only explained the past, the thinking went, but also expressed the ambitions and anxieties of the present.

But the mingling of intellectual analysis and business interests hasn’t occurred without debate: Privately owned objects aren’t subject to the same strict conservation requirements as museum artifacts. And as museums started borrowing archival pieces directly from fashion houses, sometimes a designer’s “cooperation” with an exhibition stretched to input or approval—another ethical gray area that can compromise curatorial objectivity and authority.

The ethics of fashion exhibitions got even more questionable in 2000, when the Guggenheim mounted a show about the Italian designer Giorgio Armani. The museum, which does not collect fashion, received a $15 million donation from the designer; the move was widely viewed as a transparent quid pro quo. “It’s all very well for an art gallery to declare the equality of ‘high’ and ‘low’ art forms, and to enjoy the boost in attendance that may bring,” one critic wrote at the time, “but the challenges and risks of shows like this can outweigh any benefits.”

Whether they’re focused on pants or paintings, museum exhibitions don’t just publicize and promote the work of living artists; their imprimatur actually raises its market value. The Armani show had the distinction of prompting a museum-industry trade group and the IRS to update their ethical guidelines on corporate sponsorship to encourage greater transparency.

Still, shows about living designers—produced with the help of those designers—became more common, and eventually they lost much of their stigma. For many years, in fact, the Met was one of the few holdouts. Its policy changed only when Bolton became curator in charge in 2016 and announced a show on the Japanese designer Rei Kawakubo. Bolton, according to a Times report, explicitly “wanted to challenge the idea” that museums couldn’t do monographs on living designers, and wanted to “demonstrate that ‘fashion is a living art.’” Kawakubo’s involvement was crucial to the museum’s show; every piece came from her archives, and that year, she served as the honorary chair for the Met Gala.

Galliano, with his past behavior, complicates the ethics equation even more. Museums, of course, regularly exhibit works by artists with unsavory pasts—but, crucially, those artists are usually dead. They can no longer personally profit or walk the red carpet on opening night. And unlike fine art, fashion is built in to everyday consumerism. Few people can afford to leave a museum and buy a Basquiat. Many more can pop over to Zara for a piece from Galliano’s forthcoming collection.

The art of fashion may be too enmeshed with the business of fashion for the two to ever be completely untangled. But museums can easily forestall self-inflicted scandals such as the one at the Met by not putting living designers on precarious pedestals. In the announcement of the show’s cancellation, Wintour called the move “John’s decision”; many news outlets subsequently reported that the designer “bowed out” or “withdrew” from the exhibition. This framing casts the news as Galliano’s noble self-sacrifice, and distances Wintour and the Met from the whole sorry affair. It also inadvertently highlights the conflict of interest central to this kind of show. An ethical, independent museum exhibition could have gone on without its subject’s participation. Or, better yet, it would not have sought its subject’s input in the first place.

title: The MAGA Right Is Only Pretending to Be Censored
summary: For nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case. Political appointees inside the State Department combed through old files and databases. Civil servants received notice that their personal emails would be examined. Darren Beattie—the founder of a far-right conspiracist websi...
content:
For nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case. Political appointees inside the State Department combed through old files and databases. Civil servants received notice that their personal emails would be examined. Darren Beattie—the founder of a far-right conspiracist website, then the undersecretary of state for public diplomacy—sent out a request for files on anyone who had communicated with or written about the Global Engagement Center, a now-dissolved agency that once worked to expose propaganda campaigns by Russia, China, Iran, and other countries around the world.  

[Read: The white nationalist in charge of Trump’s public diplomacy]

The request, seen last year by the MIT Technology Review, was far-reaching. Beattie was seeking information on Bill Gates; the commentator Bill Kristol; Chris Krebs, a former U.S. cybersecurity official; a German government minister; the analyst Renée DiResta, formerly at Stanford University, as well as others associated with a research project called the Election Integrity Partnership; and, as it happens, me.

This unprecedented investigation was meant to expose the Biden administration’s “censorship–industrial complex,” a shadowy network allegedly dedicated to the mass suppression of American free speech. Since 2020, internet trolls have accused Biden-administration officials, social-media companies, and university researchers of weaving a nefarious plot to censor conservatives. Since 2025, MAGA ideologues have been using this alleged plot as an excuse to dismantle government programs, stifle research, intimidate American citizens, and even distort American foreign policy.

And yet for the past year and half, neither Beattie nor anyone else has actually managed to prove that the plot ever existed. Like a soap bubble that vanishes with the touch of a hand, the “censorship–industrial complex” belongs to that mystical category of things that disappear when you examine them too closely.

The failure to produce evidence is not for lack of trying. During the Biden administration, MAGA allies and politicians filed multiple lawsuits with the goal of exposing alleged censorship. None has done so. One of them, brought by the Missouri attorney general, made it all the way to the Supreme Court before justices asked for underlying evidence that the government had censored anyone. The answer was no. Another, brought against the Stanford research project by America First Legal—Stephen Miller’s team—failed in July, when a judge found the suit had no standing, no jurisdiction, and, after a discovery process requested by the plaintiffs, no evidence. There was no proof, in other words, that the Stanford research had resulted in anyone being censored. Other cases against the Biden administration were simply settled by President Trump’s Department of Justice without finding any evidence of “censorship” either.

[Renée DiResta: My encounter with the fantasy–industrial complex]

Now the Trump administration’s most dedicated ideologues have also failed, spectacularly, to prove the existence of a “censorship–industrial complex” inside the State Department. After months of searching, Beattie’s successor as undersecretary for public diplomacy, Sarah Rogers, recently decided to publicize the unimpressive results of the inquiry into the Global Engagement Center. But instead of writing a report admitting that the documents that surfaced contained nothing of interest, she leaked them, selectively, to an internet troll known as DataRepublican.

Here is where the story becomes especially convoluted, and I will simplify as best I can. “DataRepublican” is the X pseudonym of Jennica Pounds, who has a history of misreading data and connecting dots to describe nonexistent conspiracies. But the plan went wrong: Upon receipt of raw documents from Rogers, including screenshots without context, Pounds decided that Rogers was a “Deep State” operative and refused to release them. Subsequently, it emerged that Pounds herself has been secretly employed by the Pentagon, which presumably makes her a deep-state operative too. But that’s another story.  

Because Pounds would not publish the documents, Rogers did so herself, in a long thread on X. As she must have known, they contained no evidence of conspiracy, no proof that anyone in the Biden administration censored millions or even dozens of social-media posts. Instead, Rogers, who is theoretically responsible for promoting good relations with people in foreign countries, went after a series of U.S. citizens. She found a GEC official who had about a dozen email exchanges with the Stanford project, almost all about Russian accounts. She posted a brief excerpt of the congressional testimony of Daniel Kimmage, a former State Department employee and GEC deputy coordinator, who truthfully explained that the center was set up to deal with foreign disinformation, not American media. Rogers wrote that “that was a lie,” without offering proof.

Rogers also included several misleading posts about the Stanford project, plucking a number from a table and implying that it meant the researchers had somehow targeted more than 400,000 tweets, when they in fact had merely noted their existence. More to the point, the Stanford team did so after the election, not in some kind of smoke-filled room but in an academic report that is still publicly available and that DiResta has cited repeatedly.

Rogers also criticized another very public, not remotely secret report, written jointly by the United States, Britain, Canada, Germany, Slovakia, and the European Union, investigating “gendered disinformation,” a subject that sounds very “woke” until you realize that deepfake porn videos and orchestrated misogyny are tactics regularly used against female politicians such as Annalena Baerbock, a former German foreign minister, or Giorgia Meloni, the Italian prime minister. The Iranian regime uses them to harass female dissidents around the world. Democratic governments would be negligent if they did not try to understand them. But even if you are not bothered by the online harassment of women in politics, it’s still impossible to argue that the publication of a report (and its translation into nine languages) proves the existence of a secret censorship–industrial complex stifling Americans’ views. “Watergate it was not,” Orna Blum, a former State Department official, wrote last week.

[Anne Applebaum: America surrenders in the information wars]

And if the scandal wasn’t Watergate, Rogers is not Bob Woodward. She is a public servant who dumped raw data online, seemingly without asking whether anyone would be damaged or which American foreign-policy interests could be served, all in the name of proving nothing.  

In the normal course of things the saga of the GEC documents would be, and should be, dismissed as a storm in a teapot. But unfortunately, the administration’s pursuit of a nonexistent censorship–industrial complex has already had real consequences for real people. In April 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that he was closing the Global Engagement Center because it had “spent millions of dollars to actively silence and censor the voices of Americans they were supposed to be serving.” This was untrue, and even at the time there was no evidence for such an extraordinary statement. On the contrary, the GEC was the only institution in the U.S. government that was publicly tracking hostile international information operations, including by exposing websites in Africa or Latin America that appeared local but were in fact run by Moscow or Beijing. Rubio’s statement maligned the people who worked on these reports. Will the secretary of state now apologize to them? Compensate them? Rehire them?

The closing of the center also means that no one is now doing that work. Thanks to Rogers, Beattie, and a handful of others, the U.S. decided to blind itself to the reality that Russia, China, and Iran, with its viral animated Lego videos, all run deceptive campaigns that reach millions of people around the world. And now Americans do nothing to halt, explain, or counter them.

But it is not only American foreign policy that has been damaged. Following a series of expensive lawsuits as well as public harassment, Stanford shut down its internet-monitoring projects too. DiResta, one of the most prominent scholars in the field, left the university and was subjected to years of online harassment, an experience she has previously described in The Atlantic. Other research projects across the country also suffered, as funders and university provosts were, paradoxically, scared away by the Trump administration’s threats to curtail their free speech in the name of halting “censorship.”

The study of foreign online campaigns and the proliferation of conspiracy theories has now become difficult and controversial, for people both inside and outside the government. That doesn’t mean that these campaigns don’t exist. It just means that Americans don’t know about them, don’t understand them, and cannot track them.

As if this same conspiracy theory had not done enough damage, Rogers and others at the State Department are also putting the nonexistent censorship–industrial complex at the center of American foreign policy toward Europe now too. At a conference at the Hudson Institute last spring, Rogers said that a “censorship class” had already “scuttled to Europe” to pursue a supposed vendetta against Americans from across the ocean. At the same event, Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri—who, in his previous role as the state’s attorney general, had brought one of the failed lawsuits against Stanford and supported legal challenges to the 2020 election—declared that “we are witnessing a deeply troubling assault on free speech” in Europe.  

[Conor Friedersdorf: Europe’s free-speech problem]

These views, all of which derive from the same set of false stories, are actively shaping American policy in Europe. Late last month, the State Department put forth plans to spend $4 million to support right-wing media in Europe, including a consortium of “independent journalists” who would support the Trump administration’s view of the world. In recent months, the U.S. has imposed visa restrictions on Thierry Breton, a former EU commissioner who is now a private citizen, for his role in creating the Digital Services Act, a European law designed to protect minors, provide transparency around algorithms and targeted advertising, and ensure that behavior on the internet conforms to existing legislation. The U.S. also sanctioned four European researchers who campaigned for the digital-services law or against hate speech—essentially punishing them for their free speech, in the name of promoting free speech. Two of them, the leaders of a German organization called HateAid, called the visa ban “an act of repression by a government that is increasingly disregarding the rule of law and trying to silence its critics by any means necessary.”

Belatedly, even some part of the Trump administration appears to have quietly concluded that all of this has gone too far and that maybe, in fact, it would be useful for the U.S. government to understand how hostile governments seek to manipulate the internet. In May, the State Department put out a tender for software developers who could help analyze “foreign adversarial propaganda” and thus replicate the work once done by the Global Engagement Center. In August, a State Department contractor also posted a job opening for research analysts who can, among other things, “evaluate how foreign governments, state-sponsored organizations, terrorist groups, and other malign actors use social media and digital communications to influence public opinion and targeted audiences.”

As DiResta wrote this week, “they’re hiring people to do the very job they just spent 16 months claiming was a conspiracy.” So much time, energy, and money was wasted pursuing a fiction. Now more time, energy, and money will need to be spent to clean up the damage.

content:

In this episode of The David Frum Show, The Atlantic’s David Frum opens with a discussion of how Donald Trump has enriched himself and his family during his presidencies. David discusses how these ill-gotten gains bring up difficult questions about the future of American democracy.

Then David is joined by former Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull to discuss the impact of the Trump presidency on America’s allies, its reputation around the world, and the politics in the Pacific.

Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of  Red Dawn Over China: How Communism Conquered a Quarter of Humanity, by Frank Dikötter.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Malcolm Turnbull: The United States—not by accident or circumstance, but by design—has become a less dependable ally.

[Music]

David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be former Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, and we will discuss the deterioration of the position, the strategic and economic position, of the Western democracies in the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean in the presidencies of Donald Trump. The book this week will be  Red Dawn Over China: How Communism Conquered a Quarter of Humanity. But before either the dialogue with Malcolm Turnbull or the book discussion, some opening thoughts about the question of President Trump’s wealth and what is to happen to it after he leaves office.

I wrote about this subject in The Atlantic this past weekend, and you can see my thoughts there in much more elaborated form. But there’s some major themes that I think really need to be stressed again in a very direct way, and I’d like to do that here with you now.

President Trump entered office in January 2025 as a wealthy man, as he has been almost all of his life: thanks to the great inheritance from his father, thanks to his earnings from The Apprentice and other TV programs, and thanks to some of his own business achievements. But his own business career has been one of sharp ups and downs, punctuated by bankruptcies of the businesses that he’s owned, losses to his investors. But there’s no question that he and his family are very, very wealthy today, with a fortune numbered in the multiple billions of dollars, accumulated in an astonishingly short time.

How exactly did he do that? Well, as I read it, there are three major streams of payments that he has received; three major sources of wealth that he’s received since he became president. The first takes the form of payments from people, governments, and entities with interests before the United States government. He has, for example, received large payments from American media companies. Famously, the payment from Amazon to make a documentary of his wife, Melania. Settlements from Paramount, Meta, and ABC News, money that will supposedly go to his presidential library.

He’s received gifts from foreign governments and entities as well. This stream of payments and gifts, worth many millions of dollars, has made Trump a rich man by any standard.

The second source of wealth to him has been his involvement in the cryptocurrency and other crypto-token markets, where the president has backed cryptocurrency-issuing companies. Many of the currencies and tokens that have been issued by these Trump-backed companies rapidly became worthless.

The third source has been a series of stock and other transactions in oil markets and other markets. This year, the president’s investment accounts, which the White House says are managed by third-party financial institutions, have traded oil and gas stocks. This has happened even as the president is deeply involved in the war in Iran, which has certainly had impact on this industry.

Now, America has a long tradition of letting bygones be bygones and of not looking very deeply at the activities of former presidents. But the enormous fortune that has been accumulated in such dubious ways in such a short time raises important questions. Not just about right and wrong, not just about whether individual economic laws have been obeyed, but important questions about the future of American democracy.

There are examples all over the planet of authoritarian rulers whose families accumulated enormous wealth in their time in office. The authoritarian ruler then loses power; some of the fortune is clawed back, but much is kept by the family, and that fortune becomes a basis for the family’s return to political power in a new generation. We’ve seen that in Peru with the Fujimori dynasty, in the Philippines with the Marcos dynasty. Could we see such a thing in America?

You know, the next generation of Trumps are going to inherit a lot of money, but they’re going to also inherit a lot of potential legal vulnerabilities. And one of the lessons they’ve learned from the presidency of Donald Trump is: When you have a large fortune with such a big question mark over it, one way to be safe is to reclaim political power and shut down investigations and law enforcement and accountability. And that way, the money that you achieved, whatever question marks are about it, well—no questions can be asked, because there’s no one to ask the questions.

While this enormous accumulation, rapid accumulation, of uncertain wealth remains, it continues as not just a question mark over the future of the Trump family, but a question mark over the future of American democracy. It’s a risk in a way that the wealth of the Fujimoris in Peru has been a risk, in a way that the wealth of the Marcos in the Philippines has been a risk.

Americans are not a backward-looking people. They don’t go in for retribution. In the Biden presidency, pretty clearly, Attorney General Merrick Garland wanted to stay well away from the whole Trump business, and to leave Trump as much alone as Trump’s record would possibly allow Merrick Garland to leave Trump alone.

But if there is a post-Trump administration that is concerned to restore American democracy, I don’t think that kind of averting-the-eyes method that was practiced by Merrick Garland and President Biden is safe or sustainable. To try to get to the bottom of the Trump fortune—to try to reclaim any part of it that was achieved in ways that are unlawful or improper—that’s not an act of retribution. That’s an act of democratic self-defense, and maybe, ominously, an indispensable act of democratic self-defense if the United States is not to follow the path of other failed democracies that took one blow from a first generation of an authoritarian kleptocratic family and suffered the decisive blow from the second generation.

Now, at the same time—and I’m about to do what Enoch Powell famously said politicians should never do and blame the media, but because, as he said, a politician who complains about the press is like a ship’s captain who complains about the sea—but the reality is the media, and you and I know this, having lived through it, has dramatically changed. And so what you now get is this intense competition for attention. And of course, the way people seek to achieve that, whether it’s the automatic algorithms on the social-media platforms or it’s the producers at Fox News, is by anger-tainment. And I think all of that has created this toxic brew that has been devastating for what used to be called the center right of politics.

Frum: Well, let’s do a close-up on what happened in Australia. And one of the issues that rocked your government was your attempt to reduce Australia’s quite heavy taxation of enterprises. Turnbull: David, I don’t think that’s quite right. Forgive me, but I don’t think that’s—I mean, certainly there were people that had different views.

The big divisive issue on the right of politics when I was leading the Liberal Party—and I led the Liberal Party on two occasions, in opposition and in government—was our approach to climate change. There’s no point talking about whether you believed or disbelieved in it. It was physics. But, and you’ve seen this in the U.S. in particular, you’ve got this—this was turned into a culture war. So, it was really more the bugbear that I faced with the right—and though they didn’t like the same-sex marriage legalization either, but 62 percent of the country voted for it, so it was a bit hard to argue with that politically—but the thing that was always the destabilizing issue was the approach to energy policy.

Frum: And did you find the withdrawal of American leadership on that issue made your life more complicated?

Turnbull: Yes, of course it has. Because you see, Trump and Trumpism and MAGA-ism has its imitators everywhere around the world. I mean, at the last election here in Australia, Peter Dutton, the Liberal leader who lost very badly and lost his own seat was, you know, in different ways, effectively channeling Trump.

You know, it’s very alluring, because the media is so global. Frum: But they seem to be less successful outside the United States than they are inside the United States, at least from an electoral-politics point of view.

Turnbull: Yeah. And Trump being Trumpy has not been an assistance here.

But nonetheless, these anti-science forces, this sort of algorithmic cultivation of hatred and negativity that we’re seeing now more than ever, is a challenge that I think has infected both sides of politics. But I think it’s done more damage to the sensible right.

And look, let me give you a theory of the case as someone who’s led a center-right party. My view, grounded in my own experience and observation of others, is that the center right’s political equity is economic management. You know, the left will generally be regarded as being more likely to do good things with health; even with education, with spending. The left will always be regarded as being more likely to spend more, so. And the right is often, in most countries, regarded as being a better bet on national security, but that’s rarely an election issue. Sometimes it is. But the economy obviously always is.

Now, my attitude is that the more you get sidetracked down these culture-war issues, the more you lose the time, the attention, on the one political equity you’ve got—and that’s economic management. So, you know, jobs and growth is what center-right politicians should be focused on.

Frum: But center-right politicians often nowadays seem to have lost interest in those issues. The economic management of the second Trump term has careened from higher tariffs, lower growth, lower employment, higher inflation. He’s at last paying a political price for it. Other center-right parties around the world seem to be interested in talking about immigration issues and issues of sexuality, race, of ethnic transition. That’s what gets the activists excited. That’s what the leaders respond to, and economic management goes out the window.

Turnbull: Well, all of that’s true, but let me just unpack a bit of that. I mean, the first thing you’ve got to remember about politics is that it’s a relative business. It’s like football. You may be playing in a team that is absolutely hopeless—you know, can’t catch, can’t kick, terrible. But if the people you play on the weekend are even more hopeless than you, you’ll win.

Now, the Democrats in the last election in the United States gave it to Trump. They gave it to him. I mean, their failure to secure the southern border alone was just an extraordinary abdication of responsibility. One of the fundamental things that people expect for their government is that the government should be able to determine who goes in and out of their country. Now, if you can’t do that, you’re failing in a very basic responsibility. And, you know, you’re a better assessor of this than me, David, but I would think if that had been properly addressed, I suspect even with all the other problems they had, Trump wouldn’t have been successful.

The other thing to remember too, and Australia is a little bit different. We have compulsory voting, which means everyone has to turn up to the polling place and take a ballot paper. They can write a rude word on it, or not number all the squares and cast an informal vote if they like. But we get over 90 percent of people turning up to vote, and 97 and a half percent of every eligible Australian is on the roll. So now, this means that you don’t have to run, or if you run off to the right to fire up your craziest activists, or the left for that matter, that’s not to get them out to vote. When you do that in the U.S. and many other places, that may be a legitimate strategy. Here, there’s no point, because they’re going to vote anyway. So the electoral contest is focused at the center, which is where it should be.

Frum: Well, Australia’s one of the most outward-facing economies in the world. You’re one of the most urban societies in the world. So it’s not going to work in Australia to say, Let’s put up a big fence around the country and keep out trade with everybody else, the way Americans may falsely imagine it’s plausible in the United States. So when Australians turn against the rest of the world—or when leaders invite them, political entrepreneurs, invite them to turn against the rest of the world—how does that resonate in a country that says, We can’t make a living if we’re not connected to the rest of the world?

Turnbull: Well, I mean, protectionism has never had a good—not in modern times, anyway—has never had a good degree of political support here. Generally, Australians understand free trade is good. Now, you know, obviously, the attitudes were different years ago. Decades, many decades, ago, there was protectionism. But I think all of us, pretty much, in Australia united in supporting free trade. I mean, clearly you’ve got to have fair trade. I mean, and we do have laws that deal with dumping and so forth. But generally, [in] Australia, our barriers to trade, whether it’s tariffs, are vanishingly small. We have free trade; many free-trade agreements. I mean, my government kept the Trans-Pacific Partnership alive after Trump pulled out, for example, and working with [Japanese Prime Minister] Shinzo Abe in particular to do that. So, you know, free trade is good for us, but I can understand the case they make in the U.S.

Now, you made a very good point. If I could just pick up on this, because I think it’s a really important one, particularly for an American audience and Canadian audience. Turnbull: I’m an old journalist, by the way, so. (Laughs.)

Turnbull: No.

The reality is that we have to accept the world as it is. We all have a stake in what happens in Washington, but only the Americans have a vote. Frum: You wisely caution against letting emotion dictate policy, and you mention the emotions of resentment and injury and insult, which are very real. Turnbull: David, you’re absolutely right. People who think that at the end of Trump’s current term there will be a resumption to normal transmission overlook the fact that the new normal is more or less what we have at the moment. And is a much more self-interested United States, a more protectionist United States, and a United States that is not committed to the democratic values that we’ve shared in the same way, you know, presidents of both stripes had been in years past.

Frum: And the United States, if it cannot beat Iran, probably cannot defend Taiwan.

Turnbull: Look you know, you don’t have to take my word for it. I mean, isn’t it staggering that so much of the munitions, magazines, magazine depth of the United States, it’s been depleted so considerably from this conflict with Iran? Which is not a conflict with a peer counterparty or rival, like China or Russia for that matter. This is one of the reasons I’ve been a critic of the AUKUS arrangement. It’s not being anti-American at all. My concern is that it’s a really bad deal for Australia, and we’ll end up with very little out of it.

Frum: AUKUS is an acronym for Australia, U.K., U.S.

Turnbull: Yeah. It’s a deal to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, naval nuclear propulsion. But all of it depends on the U.S. industrial base, the British industrial base—both of which are under enormous pressure and underperforming. And it’s a very, I think, very foolish sacrifice of Australian sovereignty.

Again, you can be a skeptic about the middle-power thesis of Mark Carney, right? But what’s the alternative? Is the alternative just to be a sycophantic cork, bobbing along behind the United States as it weaves from one perceived act of self-interest to another? The only alternative, difficult and complex and compromised though it may be, is to be more self-reliant and to work with other nations that have similar interests. Hence the middle-power thesis.

Frum: Let me ask you one last strategic question, which Americans tend not to think of as a strategic question, and that is the issue of corruption.

But it was still visibly within the American tradition. Corrupt millions of dollars, money going, single millions, maybe even tens of millions of dollars flowing where it shouldn’t flow. It can only be compared to a post-Soviet republic or post-colonial Africa. As Australia has many very strict rules about campaign finance. It’s a very clean country. As you view the United States as it is today, how does it affect your strategic thinking? To say the government of the United States seems to be auctioning itself off to secretive parties all over the world, in transactions that are not very legible, but that are highly suspicious and that seem to be happening in front of all of our eyes?

Turnbull: Well, look, all of this is a matter is of real concern. Obviously it’s a concern to Americans. I was at a meeting recently, in the States, with a group of senior leaders from European companies for the most part. And their big concern was that after the Trump administration, there would be a reckoning, and that there would be people who do engage in corrupt activities [who] will be brought to account. So it’s something that everyone has to think about. I mean, the—

Frum: Were they frightened of that, or were they hoping for that?

Turnbull: No, no, they were very apprehensive, very apprehensive about that. And I thought that was a good thing, because, you know, the one part of American democracy that appears to have been reasonably resilient is the justice system. Because, at the end of the day, probably the most important element in a democracy is the rule of law. A democracy that was just all about the majority getting to run the government is not much of a democracy, because the majority can win the government and then, you know, bump off the minority. So the rule of law is absolutely fundamental. And I think Americans understand that. And this perceived assault and affront to the rule of law, that will be the part of this era that is going to see, I think, the biggest, I don’t know, reckoning when it comes to an end.

At least I hope so. I hope so, because, ultimately, if you don’t have the rule of law, you don’t have trust. The rule of law and the trust that that brings is absolutely fundamental to the American economy and every modern economy. You degrade that, and you’re shooting yourself in the foot, leaving aside all of the moral and ethical issues.

Frum: You may be giving the United States’ legal system a bigger compliment than it deserves. Or maybe we need to disaggregate a little bit. I mean, it seems to be true that the courts, the federal courts, won’t convict innocent people. And when they see a blatantly unconstitutional action, like the president of the United States imposing tariffs unilaterally without the consent of Congress in clear violation of the text of the Constitution, which awards powers over tariffs and taxes to Congress, the courts will stop that.

But we’re seeing something else. I wrote about the Trump presidency at the beginning, and quoted a line I had heard when on a visit to Viktor Orbán’s Hungary in 2016. The most important or the most dangerous power in a modern bureaucratic state, where there are limits on what the government can do, is not that the justice system is abused to punish the innocent, but that the justice system is used to protect the guilty. And that does seem to be happening here. And it turns out, no, that’s not true. The system is—yes, you can’t send innocent people to prison so far, although there are innocent people who’ve been shot dead in the streets by agents of the state with no consequences, so far, to agents of the state. But we are seeing extraordinary things happen that most Americans would have supposed the president and his government can’t do. And they do it, and the courts can’t do anything, and the Department of Justice won’t do anything

Malcom Turnbull: Well, I mean, David, I’m not arguing with you. I mean, it’s not a good state of affairs, that’s for sure. But to my relief, and I imagine to your relief too, the courts have remained for the most part, including judges that have been appointed by Republican and Trump administrations, have remained resistant to what they see as abuses of power.

There’s so much wrong with the design of the American democracy. I mean, the electoral system, the gerrymandering, you know. The politicization of the judiciary. Again, Americans don’t want to hear foreigners telling them what’s wrong with their country. But look at the electoral system. Look at the way you’ve got a two-party system entrenched. It’s virtually impossible for independents to succeed. You’ve got voluntary voting. You’ve got a political culture that seems to say, at least for part of the polity, that it’s okay to discourage people from voting. It’s not made easy for people to vote. And then, you have districts gerrymandered quite deliberately so as to ensure that only one party or the other can win. And then, surprise, surprise, the only contest that matters is the primary, and surprise, surprise, people on the Democratic side win the primary by pivoting to the left, and on the Republican side by pivoting to the right or to Trump.

And, then so the general election doesn’t really matter, other than in a handful of districts. And so you end up with a Congress that is much more polarized than the country, right? I mean, whereas, what is the point of a parliament? The whole point of a parliament is to bring people together so that they compromise in the center. That’s the whole point. Otherwise, we’d just elect a dictator for four years or 10 years or something. You wouldn’t bother having a parliament. I mean, the polarization driven by the electoral system is actually defeating the very purpose of having a parliamentary system in the first place.

Frum: When you view the world from your region, does America seem as present to you as it did 10 years ago? Or does the United States feel farther away, and that other places feel bigger and more important? From an Australian point of view, is India closer, China closer, Vietnam closer than it was? More interesting, more exciting, more important, more inescapable?

Turnbull: Well, economically, India and China are vastly more important than they were 10 or 20 years ago. Certainly 20 years ago. Vastly more important. However, in terms of attention, in terms of share of mind, the United States is occupying almost everything. It’s almost impossible to not be talking about U.S. politics. I think Australians pay as much if not more attention to U.S. politics than they do to our own politics. I can only imagine that it’s even more so in Canada. The globalized media is—and we’re an example of it—has meant that the U.S. is dominating everybody’s attention. It’s like it’s sucking all the oxygen out of everywhere else. And of course, it creates a disadvantage competitively, because China has become a much less open society in the last decade or so. And so, the one thing you know is that Chinese leaders understand a lot more about how America works, a lot more than American leaders understand about how China works.

Frum: And they can do it both by open-source and by clandestine means, of which there seem to be more and more.

Turnbull: Everyone can use clandestine means. I mean, everyone gets up to that sort of stuff That’s hardly unique. But America is so open that you can—and that openness is a strength. At one level, it is a strength, I think. And who are we to decry free speech and openness? But what it does mean is that America dominates the world’s attention much more than it did a decade, let alone two decades ago, in my view.

Frum: As you travel around your region, do people still take at all seriously the ideals of America, or does it seem now a kind of bitter mockery? When the United States has just marked its 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, of those words that once seemed so resonant, does that echo? Does that still have power? Or in Vietnam, in Indonesia, even in Australia, do people say, Maybe that’s who you were, but it’s not who you are? Or do they still—does any of that confidence in what America used to be still linger in the America of today?

Turnbull: Look; everybody can distinguish between America and the American president or government for the time being. America is not defined by its president. I think the American ideals are resonant, because they are human ideals. You know—freedom, equality, life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. I mean, Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the values of the Declaration of Independence when he declared Vietnam independent after the Second World War. And he was hardly a capitalist, to say the least. So these values have been inspiring for, well, for 250 years, let’s face it. So I think they’ll remain inspiring. But I think the confidence in the United States to live up to them and to deliver on them has been undermined.

I mean, people have always been cynical. People have always said, Oh, the Americans talk about freedom and justice and democracy, but they’re really in it for themselves. Well, Donald Trump, who is in many ways refreshingly honest, makes it very clear that this is all about American self-interest. You know, that’s his slogan: “America First.” So he makes no bones about that. But what that does mean is that people have to hedge; they have to make their own arrangements. If they’re wise—not everyone is doing that; I don’t think Australia is doing enough, frankly—but if they’re wise, they should be seeking to be more independent, more self-reliant. And whether America returns to a more conventional keel, if you like, than it is on at the moment or not, I think we are all better friends of America writ large if we are more independent.

My sincere conviction—born not just out of observation, but out of real experience—is that, as a foreign leader, you are a better friend to America if you tell the truth, and a worse friend if you just join the line of backslappers and sycophants.

Frum: Malcolm Turnbull, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show.

Turnbull: Thanks, David.

Frum: Bye-bye.

[Music]

Frum:  Thanks so much to Malcolm Turnbull for joining me today on The David Frum Show. As I said at the top of the show, this week’s book is Red Dawn Over China: How Communism Conquered a Quarter of Humanity. [Frank] Dikötter is a great historian of modern China, the author of three previous books about the harrowing consequences of Mao Zedong’s rule over China: Mao’s Great Famine, The Tragedy of Liberation, and The Cultural Revolution.

That trilogy starts in 1945 and describes in detail the cost, the human cost, of Mao Zedong’s grim rule over the Chinese people. This new book, Red Dawn Over China, is a kind of prequel. It starts before 1945 and tells the story of the rise of the Chinese Communist Party to power in 1949.

Dikötter thinks there’s been a longtime myth that the Chinese Communist Party’s ascent represented some kind of popular revolution, some kind of mandate of the people. That is the thesis that Dikötter brutally takes apart in Red Dawn Over China. What he wants to show is that the Communist Party was a marginal force in Chinese life. He estimates that in 1940 the party had maybe 40,000 members in a country of half a billion people, or about one member per 1,700 people.

The Communist Party came to power in China not through a popular will, not through a popular uprising, but through a brutal campaign of terroristic violence that is largely supported by foreign efforts. That is, by the flow of money and arms from Joseph Stalin’s Soviet Union.

At the center of the story is the consequence of the Japanese invasion of China. They attacked Manchuria in 1931, and then attacked the mainland of China, the rest of China, in 1937. The Chinese nationalists, who are often presented as the villains of the story, defend the integrity of China against the foreign invaders, and pay a stupendous price in human lives and equipment to hold back the Japanese, and ultimately to be there when the Japanese are defeated by the American and Allied war against Japan.

This war leaves China in ruins. It leaves the Chinese nationalists bankrupt. It leaves their army broken. And the Communists are in position now to take over Manchuria—the former Japanese center power, adjacent to the Soviet Union, supplied by the Soviet Union, armed by the Soviet Union, paid for by the Soviet Union. And then to invade the south from the north, backed by the Soviets the whole way.

Dikötter makes the important point that at every stage of this conflict, whenever there was a flow of refugees, it was always a flow from the Communist areas to the nationalist areas, never the other way around. And when the Communists at last did seize power in 1949, it was a result not of their superior integrity, not of their superior morality, not because their arms were less corrupt, all the stories you’ve heard—it was just because they had more and better weapons provided by a more generous ally, and they had to do less for the population than the nationalists, who took more seriously than the Communists their obligations to everyday Chinese people. It’s a story, as he says, of conquest, how communism conquered a quarter of humanity.

And as we try to make sense of the kind of regime China has become, of the kind of regime that China now is, we need to always keep in mind the lesson that is taught by this book and Dikötter’s previous books. This is a regime that rests on force, on violence, and on conquest, and in no way represents the aspirations of the people it governs and misgoverns.

That’s it for this week’s David Frum Show. Thanks so much for joining. I hope you will consider subscribing to The Atlantic. That’s the best way to support the work of this program and of all of us at The Atlantic. And please share and subscribe to the program and share it on whatever social media you use. That helps to bring the program to the attention of more people.

Thanks for joining me this week. See you next week. Bye-bye.

Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.

Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

content:
• Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks

  • Airlink insists flyby conducted according to regulations

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.

Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination

A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.

Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.
